newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals -- Japan shuns some Chinese ferroalloys.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals -- Japan shuns some Chinese ferroalloys.

text.p: Supplies from the former Soviet Union and high domestic inventories have dampened Japanese interest in Chinese ferroalloys, while prices for some products could remain soft into the beginning of next year, Japanese and Chinese traders said on Tuesday.
They also said worries over product quality and reliability of delivery were making the Japanese wary of Chinese imports.
Particularly hard-hit was Chinese ferro-silicon, with offers as low as $680 to $690 a tonne, on a CIF basis at major Japanese ports, still finding little interest.
"The Japanese will diversify their sources where possible, because...there is not one major reliable producer in China," a Hong Kong trader said.
A Japanese trader at a large trade house added, "When prices are low they (the Chinese) don't ship good produce."
He said a large portion of the rising stocks at Chinese ports was poor-quality material.
He also said that some Japanese traders were trying to dump inventories, sometimes at a loss.
A rise in metal from the former Soviet Union has also been cutting into China's exports to Japan.
"Demand is falling because the Russians are taking over the market," said a source in Beijing, adding that the Chinese were now offering ferro-silicon for export at $660 to $670 a tonne.

In the fiscal year to March 31 of this year, Japan imported 304,573 tonnes of ferro-silicon from China, or 57.5 percent of total imports, although China's share in the first eight months of calendar 1996 dipped below 45 percent.
Japan imports almost all of its ferro-silicon needs.
Chinese silico-manganese exports to Japan were also suffering due to rising imports from the former Soviet Union and high domestic inventories, traders said.

One Japanese trader said inventories in Japan have been very high since July, after overbuying earlier in the year, and he expected it would take until the first quarter of next year to work them off. Some offers of $500 or less per tonne, CIF, were appearing, he said.
Prices for South African silico-manganese had yet to be set for the October-December quarter, another trader said, although he expected an agreement at around $520 to $530 per tonne, CIF.
In the ferro-chrome market as well, Chinese producers have been hit hard, traders said.
"Prices are below cost. The more they sell the more money they lose," said a Japanese trader, adding that prices for Chinese high-carbon ferro-chrome were 38-39 cents a lb or less.
South African producer prices were recently set at 42 cents a lb in quarterly negotiations with Japanese users, traders said.

One trade source in Hong Kong, however, said the Chinese were not accepting prices below this level. "The Chinese will not discount, they can't afford to," he said, adding that Chinese high-carbon ferro-chrome was currently valued around 42 to 44 cents a lb, close to the break-even point for producers.
A Chinese trader added: "China will stay on the periphery of the market and wait for the price situation to improve."
-- Edmund Klamann, Tokyo Commodities Desk +81-3-3432-6179
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Hong Kong News Desk +85-2-2843-6470
